tickets.title: Editable Prompt System with Per-Project Override
tickets.description: Extract all 8 role agent system prompts (ba, sa, pd, dev-bug, dev-feature, test, docs, sm) and the base prompt from embedded Rust string constants (`include_str!` / inline literals) into an editable `prompts/` directory with the `init` command to scaffold them, the engine to auto-discover and prefer local overrides, and graceful fallback to embedded defaults for projects without overrides. The file layout should be `prompts/_base.md` + `prompts/{ba,sa,pd,dev_bug,dev_feature,test,docs,sm}.md` + `prompts/onboarding/{po_interview,sa_archaeology}.md` + `prompts/discussion.md` per PLAN.md §3j. Goal it serves: enables users to customize agent behavior per project — essential for adoption in real codebases where LLM output quality varies and domain conventions differ. Without this, every customization requires forking or editing Rust source. Edge cases: missing prompt files fall back silently to embedded defaults (not a hard error), partial overrides are valid (user can override just `ba.md` and keep the rest embedded), and the engine caches resolved prompt paths at startup to avoid per-call stat() on every agent run.

technical.approach:
Layered prompt resolution with per-project override store, following the config's existing per_role pattern.

LAYERING:
domain (crates/domain/src/prompts.rs): PromptKey enum (Po, Sm, Ba, Sa, Pd, Dev, Test, Docs, Base, Standards), Prompt entity (id/key, content, version), PromptVariant enum (Role, Base, Standards, Constraint).

application:
- Use cases (crates/application/src/use_cases/prompts/): ListPrompts, GetPrompt, CreateOrUpdatePrompt, DeletePrompt, ResolveEffectivePrompt, PreviewPromptUseCase
- Prompt store port (crates/application/src/ports/outbound/prompt_store.rs): async trait with load/save/delete/query
- Composition (prompts.rs updated): system_prompt() accepts optional project overrides; prompt resolution merges BASE→project-base-override→standards→project-standards-override→role→project-role-override→constraints

infrastructure:
- JsonPromptStore adapter (crates/infrastructure/src/): stores overrides in per-project .coxagent/prompts/*.md files, reads/writes via workspace files port
- PromptEntity type for serde (prompt_id, key, variant, content, version, created_at, updated_at)

presentation:
- HTTP endpoints in server.rs: GET/POST/PATCH/DELETE /api/projects/:id/prompts?filter=role|base|standards, POST /api/projects/:id/prompts/preview (dry-run resolution)
- Prompt listing, editing, and preview

NON-FUNCTIONALS:
- Authz: admin/editor only; PO can view only
- Validation: content-length capped at 4000 chars, mandatory fields non-empty, no shell metacharacters in constraint blocks
- Observability: every prompt change logged in activity feed
- Rollback: soft-delete + version history (last 5 per key)

SERVICE SPLIT: none — prompt management is part of the application domain, shared with project config, and the JSON store uses the same workspace path. No independent scale/deploy need.

CONCRETE PLAN:
1. domain: PromptKey + PromptVariant enums, Prompt entity, PromptError
2. ports: PromptStorePort trait
3. use_cases: List/Get/UpS/Delete/Resolve/Preview
4. infrastructure: JsonPromptStore adapter, serde types
5. presentation: HTTP handlers
6. prompts.rs: update system_prompt() to accept optional project overrides
7. Test: unit per tier + integration (store→use case) + e2e (HTTP→store)
files: crates/domain/src/prompts.rs — PromptKey, PromptVariant enums, Prompt entity, PromptError
crates/application/src/prompts.rs — update system_prompt() to accept project overrides

New: .coxagent/prompts/ directory per project
- Schema: per-PromptKey JSON files (e.g. po.json, sm.json)
  { prompt_id: uuid, key: PromptKey, variant: enum, content: string, version: u64, archived: bool, archived_at: option(tz), created_at: tz, updated_at: tz, history: [{version, content, archived, archived_at}] }
- Soft-delete: archived=true, archived_at=now(); last 5 revisions kept in history
- No DB migration (local JSON store, not Postgres yet)

tickets.title: Automated Visual QA Pipeline
tickets.description: Automate the PD design-QA gate using the existing multimodal engine capability: after TEST verifies a feature builds and functional smoke passes, the pipeline automatically generates screenshots and runs the PD agent to compare against the feature's `design.ux` spec (screens/routes specified, component states expected) and the project's `design_system.md` (tokens, components, patterns). This closes the M6 gap where PD UX authoring exists but automated design consistency checking does not. Goal it serves: ensures the shipped UI matches the design intent without requiring human review of every screenshot — a critical quality gate for products with UI. The output goes on the ticket thread as DoD evidence (screenshot + pass/fail + specific design violations), making design QA as automated and traceable as the functional smoke.js gate. Edge cases: features with `has_ui=false` skip the pipeline entirely, a missing or empty `design.ux` on a UI feature blocks the pipeline (returns to SA), and the pipeline tolerates legitimate design iteration (PD can update `design_system.md` as part of the same cycle if the design evolved).
acceptance_criteria: After TEST verifies a feature with `has_ui=true`, the pipeline automatically captures screenshots of all routes described in the feature's `design.ux` spec

The PD agent evaluates screenshots against `design_system.md` (palette, typography, component patterns) and `design.ux` (expected screens, component states) and posts pass/fail findings on the ticket thread
Missing `design.ux` on a UI feature causes the visual QA stage to skip without failing — the ticket proceeds but the SA preflight detects the gap and requests UX design before DEV proceeds
Features with `has_ui=false` or `complexity=small` are excluded from the visual QA pipeline per config
Visual QA results are persisted as evidence attachments on the ticket and are includable in the DOCS agent's input for user guide generation (e.g., documenting known design deviations)

tickets.title: TL Project Activation & Walking Skeleton
tickets.description: The TL project exists in deployed state with a bare `project_context.md` and one pending chore (TL-C001 'Dockerize for deploy') but zero real work. This proposal defines the first productive cycle for this project: a minimal 'hello-world' service with `/health` endpoint, Docker Compose file that actually works, and a smoke test that proves it runs — per PLAN.md §3g (walking skeleton as the seed). Goal it serves: demonstrates the autonomous team actually delivers value on a real project (not just test fixtures), validates the end-to-end pipeline (BA proposes → SA designs → DEV implements → TEST verifies → DOCS documents), and produces the concrete foundation the backlog should grow from. Unlike generic backlog items, this is a concrete activation scenario for the only deployed project. Dependencies: requires the prompt system (proposal 1) to have usable role prompts, requires the deploy adapter to work in the current environment, and requires TEST to produce actionable bug tickets from the baseline. Edge cases: the baseline test may find real bugs in the current codebase that must be addressed before proceeding (the brownfield baseline protocol in PLAN.md §3g), and the Docker deployment must not bind the hub port (COXAGENT_PORT or deploy.host_port safety).

technical.approach:
TL Walking Skeleton — minimal end-to-end execution path.

Architecture decisions:
- Layering: tl-ast (data) → tl-lexer/tl-parser (analysis) → tl-hir (desugaring) → tl-typecheck (validation) → tl-interpreter (execution). Interpreter-based execution for the skeleton (no codegen/LLVM needed).
- Module boundaries: Use existing crates. No new crate — only glue at tl-driver and examples.
- Pattern: Compiler pipeline as a series of pure transforms, each returning (Result, Diagnostics). Evaluator as mutable state machine over expression tree.
- Non-functionals:
  - Security: sandboxed execution via Rust runtime (no arbitrary syscalls), no FFI until Phase 3+
  - Failure modes: diagnostic accumulation throughout pipeline; fatal at each stage on Error severity
  - Observability: per-stage timings (--timings), stderr diagnostics, stdout program output
  - Migration: none needed (new code only)
- Service split: single binary (tl-driver) — one file handles all commands; no service boundary exists at this stage.

Concrete plan:
1. Create `examples/walking-skeleton.tn` — minimal TL program exercising let, binary ops, loop, println, if/else, block return:
   - Variables: `let x = 42`, `let greeting = "Hello"`
   - Loops: `while` loop counting to 10
   - Conditionals: `if/else` branching
   - Output: `println` with multiple args
   - Functions: `fn foo(x: Int) -> Int` call
   - Block tail return: expression without semicolon returns value
2. Add `tests/walking_skeleton.rs` to tl-driver with:
   - `fn walking_skeleton_runs_clean()` — runs `tl run examples/walking-skeleton.tn`, asserts exit code 0, validates expected output lines
   - `fn walking_skeleton_lexes()` — `tl lex` produces tokens without errors
   - `fn walking_skeleton_parses()` — `tl parse` produces AST without errors  
   - `fn walking_skeleton_types()` — `tl typecheck` passes
3. Add `scripts/activate.sh` — project activation script:
   - Verifies Rust 1.85+ toolchain (rust-toolchain.toml)
   - Builds workspace: `cargo build --workspace`
   - Runs walking skeleton: `cargo run --bin tl -- run examples/walking-skeleton.tn`
   - Reports activation success/failure
4. Create `rust-toolchain.toml` with `channel = "1.87"` (per workspace config)
5. Create justfile if missing with: `check`, `test`, `skeleton` targets

Output: a user can run `activate.sh`, see the walking skeleton execute, and read test output confirming pipeline stages pass.
technical.api_contract:
No external API surface. Walking skeleton defines the CLI interface:

```bash
# Activation
toolchain = "rust 1.85+"
target = "cargo build --workspace && cargo test --workspace"

# Walking skeleton execution
tl run examples/walking-skeleton.tn           # -> expected output + exit 0

# Individual pipeline stages (for diagnosis)
tl lex examples/walking-skeleton.tn           # -> tokens + exit 0  
tl parse examples/walking-skeleton.tn         # -> AST + exit 0
tl typecheck examples/walking-skeleton.tn     # -> "typecheck: ok" + exit 0

# Timings
tl run --timings examples/walking-skeleton.tn # -> output + per-stage ms
```

Diagnostic interface: JSON format via --message-format json (used in tests):```json
{"severity": "error|warning|note", "message": "...", "span": {"start": u32, "end": u32}}
```

- `rust-updated.toml.lock` (if rustup downloads toolchain)

1. `fn walking_skeleton_runs_clean()`:

   - Assert: exit code 0, output contains expected lines, stderr empty on success

2. `fn walking_skeleton_lexes()`:
   - Run: `tl lex examples/walking-skeleton.tn`
   - Assert: exit code 0, stdout contains token listings

3. `fn walking_skeleton_parses()`:
   - Run: `tl parse examples/walking-skeleton.tn`
   - Assert: exit code 0, stdout contains "Program {" (AST dump)

4. `fn walking_skeleton_types()`:

   - Assert: exit code 0, stdout contains "typecheck: ok"

5. `fn skeleton_times_pipeline_stages()`:  
   - Run: `tl run --timings examples/walking-skeleton.tn`
   - Assert: timing table shows lex, parse, hir, typecheck, codegen stages with ms values

6. `fn skeleton_produces_json_diagnostics()`:
   - Run bad file with --message-format json
   - Assert: stderr is valid JSON array of diagnostic objects

Expected output of walking-skeleton.tn:
```
Hello, TL! (42)
Sum of 1..10: 55
10 is even
foo(3) = 6
42 is large
```

Pre-requisite: `cargo test --workspace` passes baseline (1240+ tests)
technical.alternatives:
Considered/rejected:

1. **Direct LLVM codegen path (skip interpreter)** — rejected: codegen/LLVM backend not stable, adds clang dependency, hides language issues behind codegen bugs. Interpreter is the authoritative semantics for Phase 0-2.

2. **Separate analysis phases (tl-lex, tl-parse, tl-run as separate binaries)** — rejected: complicates activation with too many moving parts. Single `tl run` command with --timings gives same diagnostic capability.

3. **Full feature showcase as skeleton** — rejected: actors, SQL, CRDTs all depend on runtime not yet stable. Skeleton must verify basics first; feature exercises come later as individual example files.

tickets.title: Test Coverage Gap Detection
tickets.description: The TEST role runs tests but has zero awareness of test coverage — it files bugs on failures but never identifies untested code. The BA cannot propose test improvement tickets because no coverage data exists. This feature adds a coverage analysis step that runs after DEV ships code: scan source files to identify functions/modules with no `#[test]`/`def test_`/equivalent, cross-reference against ticket evidence and deploy history, then auto-propose low-priority chore tickets for the highest-coverage-gap areas. It advances two lines of the product goal: (1) the autonomous team’s self-improvement — the BA gets structured data to propose meaningful test tickets instead of generic "write tests" filler, and (2) any project managed by CoXAgent inherits this capability. Edge cases: platform-gated code (macOS-only helpers via `#[cfg(target_os = "macos")]`) should be excluded from gap analysis; test-only files already satisfy coverage for the production files they import; inline test modules (the `#[cfg(test)]` pattern already tracked in `run_dev/gates.rs`) are respected. Dependencies: builds on the existing `tests/` gate infrastructure and the `run_dev/gates.rs` inline-test detection logic. Risk/open question: coverage scanning is a compile/runtime concern — should it run via a lightweight pass (AST-based function-to-test mapping, no binary needed) or require compiling with coverage flags? AST-based is cheaper but misses branch-level granularity; the MVP should be AST-line coverage (function existence + call graph reachability) which is sufficient for ticket prioritization.

technical.approach: Static coverage-gap detection built on the existing code graph (CodeGraph, ts.rs symbol extraction) plus test-symbol extraction, not dynamic instrumentation.

acceptance_criteria: Coverage analysis identifies all top-level functions in production source files that have no test file importing or calling them, and reports them grouped by module.
Platform-gated functions (e.g. cfg-gated for specific OS) are excluded from coverage gaps when the test runner is not on that platform.
The BA auto-proposes chore tickets for the top uncovered modules when coverage gaps exceed a configurable threshold (default: any module with >3 uncovered functions).
Existing coverage patterns are respected: inline `#[cfg(test)]` modules satisfy coverage for their host file, and test files that import production symbols mark them as covered.

tickets.title: Automated Release Pipeline
tickets.description: Milestones track target versions, deploy history records every shipped ticket, and the changelog renders deterministically from history — but there is no mechanism to actually CREATE a release when a milestone's target version is reached. The PO sets milestones but nothing bridges the gap between 'version is achieved in history' and 'a release exists.' This feature auto-triggers a release artifact when all milestone targets have been shipped: it creates a tag from the milestone's `target_version`, assembles release notes from the changelog filtered to that version's range, posts them to the team channel, and creates a 'Release vX.Y.Z' chore ticket with all producing ticket IDs as a reference. It advances the product goal by making the autonomous team fully autonomous through delivery: the team proposes → designs → builds → verifies → documents → releases, without human orchestration needed for the final step. Edge cases: a milestone may have multiple target versions (e.g. 'reach v1.2.0 by Q3'); only milestone targets that are >= current_version should trigger releases; if a release tag already exists, the pipeline should skip rather than conflict. Dependencies: reads from `milestones`, `history`, and `config.workflow`; writes to git via existing `GitPort`. Risk: automated tagging is a high-trust operation — should require a config toggle (`releases.enabled`) since it mutates the git history of the managed codebase.

(3) On a failed deploy (health probe down, image failed, compose error — the exact scenario of the 10 failed fleet-wide compose deploys), the pipeline rail falls red at the failing stage and the banner flips to a failure message in plain language, never a raw error code: 'Deploy failed — service orders-api never answered /health after 60s'. (4) Rollback flow: a one-click confirm dialog restates the target and consequence ('Restores 8f21c3, released Aug 4 14:02. This will run build + health gate again') then runs the pipeline against that sha; when complete the rails shows ROLLED-BACK/REDEPLOYED with a teal badge and the previously-green sha back on top of the timeline. (5) If the last good is stale (> max_rollback_age) or ships an unreconciled DB migration, the button is disabled with an explanation-so-the-user-isn't-stranded: 'Rollback unavailable — last known good is 6 days old' with a link to the Operations runbook. Non-admin viewers see the same view read-only (no rollback/rerun actions); there is no build-trigger button because the pipeline is fully automated — the user's job is to watch, intervene only on failure, and roll back when a release breaks.
screens: Releases (primary) — current release pipeline rail: Live banner (sha + version + Live/Stage/FAILED state); stages Gates → Lint/Tests → Build → Deploy → Health Probe each with icon, duration, status badge (passing green / running teal spinner / failed red / waiting muted), and expandable log line on failure. Timeline of prior releases (newest first): per-row version, sha, shipped-by, elapsed, outcome chip (Live / Rolled-back teal / Failed red), deploy_index ordinal. Header: project name + 'Releases' tab, role-aware actions (Roll back / Rerun failed stage for admins; read-only for viewers).

Overview (home) — compact Release widget in the health card cluster replacing the single 'Deployment healthy/failed' line. Live stage dot + text ('Probing health…' / 'Live · 8f21c3' / 'Deploy failed — roll back'), 'Last good <sha>', one-tap deep link to Releases. Same data, no duplication of the full rail.

Rollback confirm dialog — inline modal: 'Roll back to <sha>?' with plain-language consequence, target known-good summary, age, and a migration-safety warning when present ('A DB migration shipped after this good build — rolling back may need the schema restored'). Confirm rolls; Cancel closes; Esc/click-out closes; focus trapped; Enter confirms.

Release detail / failure drill-in — when a stage fails, the failing stage expands to show the bounded error lines with a plain-language explainer + Next step ('Check the health endpoint' / 'Try the build locally with docker compose up before pushing' — echoing the team lesson that compose must pass locally before push). Copy-log + link to the live operator log (already viewable per-operator in the dashboard).

Pipeline stage row: passing (green check, time), running (teal spinner, pulse), failed (red x + expandable error), skipped (muted dash, e.g. 'no tests'), queued/waiting (muted 'waiting on previous'), idle (muted). Disabled state: show only when action gating is needed — stages are not manually clickable for viewers.
